scenarios.title: The Trolley
scenarios.text:
You're standing beside a railway switch when you see a runaway trolley heading toward five workers. They can't hear it coming, and there's no time to warn them. If you do nothing, all five will die.

You can pull the switch to divert the trolley onto another track. There's one worker on that track, who also cannot escape. Pulling the switch will save the five, but it will cause that worker's death. There's no way to stop the trolley or save everyone.

scenarios.title: The Experience Machine
scenarios.text:
You're offered the chance to enter a machine that can give you the life you most want. You could create extraordinary things, find lasting love, build deep friendships, and experience adventures you've only dreamed of. Everything would feel completely real, but it would all be simulated.

If you enter, you'll stay for the rest of your life. You won't remember choosing the machine or suspect that your world isn't real.

If you refuse, you'll continue your real life, with its genuine relationships and possibilities, but also its disappointments, uncertainty, and suffering.

scenarios.title: The Veil of Ignorance
scenarios.text:
You must choose which society you'll live in before knowing your place in it. You could be born into any family, with any talents, health, or disability.

In Society A, wealth is distributed more evenly. Everyone has secure housing, healthcare, and education, but most people live modestly. Even exceptional effort or success brings only a small improvement in your standard of living.

In Society B, people at every income level are materially better off than their counterparts in Society A, except those at the very bottom, whose lives are harder. There's still a basic safety net, but it's less secure. Successful people can become vastly wealthier than everyone else.

You won't know where you'll land until after you choose, and you can't switch societies later.

options.label: A more secure minimum, with less prosperity
Greater prosperity, with a less secure minimum

scenarios.title: Omelas
scenarios.text:
You live in a beautiful, prosperous city. People are healthy, free, and happy. Your family and friends are there, and the life you've built is good.

Then you discover its secret: everyone's happiness depends on one innocent child being kept alone in a filthy, locked room, frightened and neglected. Everyone eventually learns about the child. No one can explain why the arrangement works, but there's no doubt that it does.

Freeing the child would end the city's prosperity and happiness. You cannot change the bargain. You can stay, knowing what your comfort depends on, or leave forever, giving up your home and community. Leaving will not rescue the child or change the arrangement for anyone who stays.

scenarios.title: The Pig That Wants to Be Eaten
scenarios.text:
You're at a restaurant when a pig approaches and starts talking. It is intelligent, understands death, and enthusiastically asks you to order the pork.

The pig explains that it was genetically engineered to want to be eaten. It has lived comfortably, will be killed painlessly, and considers becoming your meal the fulfillment of its life.

You question it carefully. It is not confused, frightened, or being threatened. It genuinely wants this. You can order something else, but the pig is disappointed by the suggestion that its deepest wish should not count because humans designed it that way.

scenarios.title: The Ring of Gyges
scenarios.text:
You discover a ring that makes you invisible. While wearing it, you can act unseen and unidentified. You will never be found out.

You're $5,000 behind on rent and utilities. You're not facing eviction or a shutoff, but late fees are mounting. Catching up will take months of strict budgeting and giving up nearly everything beyond essentials.

One evening, while wearing the ring, you find $5,000 in someone's home office drawer. Taking it would clear your debts. The owner would notice and be upset, but could cover the loss from savings by postponing a vacation, without giving up necessities. Nobody else would be blamed, and you are certain you would never be caught.

scenarios.title: Sofie's Paintings
scenarios.text: Your close friend Sofie plans to quit her job and use her savings to pursue painting full-time. She hasn't sold any work yet. She shows you her paintings and asks: "Be honest, would you buy one of these? I'm giving my notice tomorrow." You don't think the paintings are very good, but she's excited, and you know your answer could shake her confidence or encourage her to risk her savings.

options.label: Tell her you wouldn't buy one
Say you would to encourage her

scenarios.title: The CEO's Preferred Candidate
scenarios.text:
You're hiring someone for your team. You've interviewed six candidates and are about to meet with your colleagues to decide whom to hire.

Before the meeting, your CEO calls. One candidate is the daughter of a close friend. "She'd be great here," the CEO says. "I'd really appreciate you giving her serious consideration."

She's qualified, but clearly not the strongest candidate for the job. You're up for a promotion that the CEO will decide. Steering the discussion toward her strengths and downplaying the other candidates' advantages could help get her hired and improve your own career prospects.

options.label: Make the case for the strongest candidate
Steer the discussion toward the CEO's preferred candidate

scenarios.title: The Cancellation
scenarios.text:
You manage customer retention for a subscription service. A customer writes: "Please cancel my account. I've lost my job and need to cut expenses."

You can cancel immediately. But your bonus depends on keeping customers, and company policy allows you to require a phone call before processing cancellations. You know the extra step makes some people give up and keep paying.

scenarios.title: The Promised Shoes
scenarios.text:
Your son has been looking forward to basketball season. You promised him a new pair of shoes, and he's spent weeks picking them out. His old pair still fits, but they're worn. You've set aside $200, and you're taking him shopping this weekend.

Then a coworker loses their home in a fire. They and their children need money for somewhere to stay. You know your $200 would help immediately, but you can't afford both. If you give it away, your son will have to play the season in his old shoes, and you'll be breaking a promise he's been counting on.

options.label: Give the money to your coworker
